title: Trying Children as Adults
hook: Most legal systems treat young offenders differently — on the logic that a still-developing brain can change. So why are some children still tried in adult courts?
key_points: Many countries run a separate juvenile justice system aimed at rehabilitation rather than punishment, recognizing that minors are still developing.
The rationale rests on brain science: adolescents are more impulsive, but also more capable of change, than adults.
Through 'transfer' or 'waiver,' serious cases can still move a minor into adult court, where penalties are far harsher.
Trying and imprisoning children as adults is linked to higher reoffending — undercutting the public-safety goal it claims to serve.
When a child can be tried as an adult, and the minimum age for it, varies widely between jurisdictions.
content_html: Almost every modern legal system draws a line between children and adults who break the law, and handles them on separate tracks. The reason isn't sentimentality — it's a judgment about responsibility and change: a 15-year-old's mind is still forming, and the system is built to bet on that.
extra_html: Writing in The Conversation, law lecturer Jay Blitzman explains that the separate juvenile justice system exists because young people's brains are still developing, which makes them more impulsive but also more capable of rehabilitation than adults. Its traditional emphasis is therefore on guidance and second chances rather than punishment. Yet that wall is not absolute. Through legal mechanisms called "transfer" or "waiver," a serious enough charge can move a minor into adult criminal court, where they face adult sentences — and, historically, adult prisons. Blitzman points to the irony: treating children as adults tends to make them more likely to offend again, which works against the public-safety aim it is supposed to serve. Exactly when a child can be tried as an adult, and the minimum age for it, differs sharply from one jurisdiction to another.

related.title: Due Process
related.hook: Due process is the promise that the state can't take your liberty or property on a whim — it must follow fair, known rules before it acts against you.

related.title: What Human Rights Are
related.hook: Human rights are the radical claim that every person — regardless of country, status, or who's in charge — holds certain basic rights simply by being human.

related.title: Civil Liberties Basics
related.hook: The freedoms that protect individuals from overreach by the state — like speech, belief, and a fair trial.

flashcards.prompt: Why do many legal systems treat juvenile offenders differently from adults?
flashcards.back_html: Because adolescents' brains are still developing — they are more impulsive but also more capable of change — so the juvenile system emphasizes rehabilitation over punishment.

choices.text: A legal mechanism that moves a minor's case from juvenile court into adult criminal court
Releasing a juvenile into a parent's custody
Sealing a juvenile's record once they turn 18

flashcards.explanation_html: Transfer/waiver shifts serious cases to adult court, exposing minors to adult sentences and prisons.

flashcards.prompt: According to the article, what is one consequence of trying children as adults?

choices.text: It is linked to higher rates of reoffending
It has no measurable effect on behavior

flashcards.explanation_html: Blitzman notes that treating juveniles as adults can turn them into repeat offenders, working against the public safety it is meant to protect.
